<reason>Side A built the sharper frame early — the "bare yes vs. enriched consent" dilemma and the pharmacy case were live threats, and the landlord pressure question was genuinely damaging. But Side B handled every pressure point with principled answers: the third horn (coercion by the transacting party vs. hard circumstances) blunted the dilemma, the threat/offer and baseline-entitlement analysis cleanly convicted the landlord, and the closing landed the unrebutted point that A's "exit" criterion collapses into voluntariness itself — A never answered that collapse. A's remaining meta-argument (B keeps redefining consent, proving the motion) was rhetorically powerful and B's pharmacy bullet carries real intuitive cost, but B's moral-vs-policy-verdict defense plus the shortage mechanism gave a coherent reason to accept it. B's position was stated in the opening, not invented late, and was consistently refined rather than swapped. B made the debate easier to decide and answered more of the direct pressure; A's strongest cards were absorbed rather than neutralized but left fewer unanswered burdens on B's side. Minor clipping on B's turns was a small execution cost, not enough to flip the call.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The landlord exchange: A's Q1 crafted a truthful, non-threatening predator that seemed to pass B's "seller didn't cause the desperation" test; B's A1/A2 answered with the threat/offer distinction — degrading an existing entitlement versus declining to confer a benefit — converting A's trap into a categorical line, then turning it around by showing A's own "exit" criterion was voluntariness restated.</best_rebuttal>
